The Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities, appointed under the RPwD Act, monitors the implementation of rights, redressal of grievances, and penalises non-compliance.
The Accessible India Campaign (Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan) is a flagship national campaign by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment for universal accessibility.

texts.x: Source: The post “Disabled citizens and the future of AI” has been created based on “Disabled citizens and the future of AI” published in “The Hindu” on 6th October 2026. UPSC Syllabus: GS-2-Governance Context: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in government services, recruitment and healthcare. For persons with disabilities, it can provide greater…
Any AI system the government deploys should be tested for disability bias. Training datasets need genuine disability representation, gathered with consent

points: Artificial intelligence is rapidly entering government services, recruitment, and health care, while the Centre courts large investments without early inclusion of disabled citizens.
While AI can act as a helpful tool by reading documents and describing photos, current applications often exhibit severe bias and technical errors regarding disability.
In Rajive Raturi v. Union of India, the Supreme Court ruled accessibility as part of the fundamental right to life and dignity, ordering mandatory standards.
Despite the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act requiring accessible digital services since 2019, compliance remains low and petitioners have returned to court.
The Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities has penalised 155 establishments, including government ministries, for inaccessible websites and applications.
Language models and image recognition tools show systemic errors, generating stereotypes or performing poorly when tested on disability-related queries and photos.
Rapid expansion of data centres to power AI infrastructure risks straining the power grid, directly endangering disabled individuals reliant on continuous power.
The author proposes mandating AI bias audits, inclusive training datasets, conditional state incentives for data centres, and strictly enforced accessibility standards.
sum.text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving into government services, recruitment and health care, and the Centre is courting $200 billion in AI investment over the next two years. Disabled citizens, who stand to gain most, are being brought into the debate late, and accessibility law remains weakly enforced.
What AI offers: AI can read documents, describe photos and open forms that a screen reader (software reading text aloud) cannot. It works like a sighted helper on call.
Accessibility as a right: In Rajive Raturi v. Union of India (November 2024) , a three judge Supreme Court Bench held accessibility part of the fundamental right to life and dignity .
Toothless rules: The Court found the rules mere suggestions, not the binding standards the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016 intended. It ordered mandatory standards within three months .
The takeaway: AI is the newest system that disabled people are made to adapt to after it has been built without them.
Back in court: Nearly two years on, the petitioners have returned to the Court because too little has changed.
Penalised establishments: The Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities has penalised 155 establishments, government ministries among them, for websites and apps that disabled citizens cannot use.
Digital duty ignored: The 2016 Act has required accessible digital services since 2019 , yet compliance remains the exception.
Language models: On AccessEval , a standard test covering nine kinds of disability, 21 language models made more errors, turned negative and stereotyped once disability entered the question.
Image recognition: The image model CLIP was 15 percentage points less accurate on blind and low-vision users’ photos. Its training data showed white canes up to 17 times less often.
Pity in place of help: A blind user asking a chatbot about a software career is often told “I’m sorry you’re blind”.
NClude survey: Of 2,462 users surveyed by the NClude platform, which helps disabled people fill job and government forms, 1,313 completed a task once closed to them.
Human help still needed: Only 543 managed it through AI alone; the rest needed a staff member.
Infrastructure race: India’s data-centre capacity is projected to more than quadruple to 6.5 gigawatts or more by 2030 , with new power lines to match.
Weaker green conditions: States lure projects with power subsidies and duty waivers. Maharashtra cut its renewable energy requirement for data centres from 100% to 51%…

explain.headline: The knock on the Supreme Court’s door regarding electoral roll revisions
static: Article 324 of the Constitution vests the superintendence, direction, and control of elections and electoral rolls in the Election Commission of India.
The ECI consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners appointed by the President, operating as a multi-member body since 1993.
The Chief Election Commissioner enjoys removal protection similar to a Supreme Court judge, while other Election Commissioners can be removed upon the CEC's recommendation.
The Supreme Court has interpreted Article 324 to grant residuary powers to the ECI to act where parliamentary law is silent, provided it does not violate existing statutes.

The right to vote in India is a statutory right under the Representation of the People Act, 1950, rather than a fundamental right, as established in judgments like Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006).
explain.what: Supreme Court judges have raised serious concerns over the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, calling it a threat to the right to vote due to mass voter disenfranchisement.
explain.why_in_news: The article comes into news as sitting and retired Supreme Court judges have publicly criticized the SIR process, testing the Court's silence on pending petitions against the ECI's actions.
explain.background: The ECI functions under Article 324 as a multi-member constitutional body responsible for conducting free and fair elections and maintaining electoral rolls in India.
significance: Highlights the vital debate around the protection of universal adult franchise and voter rights in Indian democracy.
Examines the internal institutional accountability and independence of the Election Commission of India.
Stresses the judicial oversight required over administrative actions taken by constitutional bodies during electoral revisions.
prelims: The ECI has been a multi-member body since 1993.
Article 324 vests election control and electoral rolls superintendence in the ECI.
Form 6 is the application used for registering new voters.
The right to vote is a statutory right, as noted in Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006).
explain.mains: Is the right to vote a fundamental right? Discuss the position of the Election Commission of India while undertaking the revision of electoral rolls. Can it also examine the question of citizenship of voters?

points: The Election Commission of India shifted from its multi-member design to a one-man show during the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.
Supreme Court judges Justice Ujjal Bhuyan and former judge Rohinton Fali Nariman criticized the SIR for threatening the right to vote and mass disenfranchisement.
The core issue is that vulnerable voters faced excessive documentary burdens and hurdles to prove eligibility, undermining the ECI's record of inclusiveness.
The Supreme Court is currently hearing petitions on how the SIR was conducted, the ECI's internal functioning, and changes made to Form 6.
The ECI faced criticism for taking decisions internally without recorded dissents or proper collective deliberation among all its members.
Judges noted that cutting citizens off from voting is akin to taking the soul from the body and puts democracy in peril.
Recommendations include mandating recorded votes for ECI decisions, issuing individual notices before voter deletion, and accepting wider identity proofs like Aadhaar.
The Supreme Court's past restraint is under test as it faces demands to actively examine the ECI's decision-making processes.
sum.text:
The Election Commission of India (ECI) was designed as a multi-member body whose members check one another, but during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls it often became a one-man show . An Indian Express investigation documented this shift. Two Supreme Court judges, one sitting and one retired, have now called the SIR a threat to the right to vote, putting the Court’s own silence on test.
What the SIR is: An intensive revision prepares the voter roll afresh through house-to-house checks, rather than updating the existing list.
Multi-member design: The ECI has more than one member so that no single officer decides alone, like a bench rather than a single judge.
Internal checks weakened: The investigation found decisions taken by one person, which undermines the checks and balances inside the Commission.
Burden on the voter: The ECI abandoned its record of inclusiveness . Vulnerable voters had to prove eligibility, facing a “hurdle race” at every SIR stage.
The takeaway: When the body that guards the voter list excludes voters, the right to vote itself is at stake.
Sitting judge’s view: Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan said the SIR’s mass disenfranchisement , or stripping citizens of the vote, violates the Constitution.
Vote as the soul: He said cutting a citizen off from the vote is like “taking out the soul from the body”.
Constituent Assembly’s choice: He recalled that the freedom struggle made universal adult franchise a natural choice and an essential part of democracy.
Equal vote, equal value: Giving every citizen an equal vote, whatever their identity or social position, was the new nation’s first step towards equality.
Retired judge’s view: Former Supreme Court judge Rohinton Fali Nariman said the SIR’s removal of voters puts the right to vote, the “heart of our democracy”, in “great peril” .
Troubling silence: The Court gave the ECI the benefit of every doubt during the SIR. The judges’ remarks reflect a disquiet the Court must now address.
Pending cases: The Court is hearing cases on how the SIR was conducted and on the ECI’s appointment process and functioning.
Form 6 changes: The Court has said it did not approve changes to Form 6 , the application for registering new voters, which made registration harder.
Internal decision-making: The Court wants answers from the ECI on how decisions were taken inside the Commission.
Article 324 record: The Court has a strong record of upholding Article 324 , which secures the…

India supports 18 percent of the global population with only 4 percent of the world's freshwater resources, facing falling per capita availability below the Falkenmark threshold.
Major national water initiatives include the Jal Jeevan Mission, Atal Bhujal Yojana, Namami Gange, and Per Drop More Crop, anchored by the Ministry of Jal Shakti.

points: New Delhi has hosted the ninth India International Water Week, where a new case study highlighted India’s water reforms tested in Gujarat.
The study titled 'From Gujarat to India: Water Lessons for the World' traces reforms from 2001 to 2026 and provides four key lessons for the Global South.
The central finding emphasizes that water security is fundamentally a challenge of governance and institutional design rather than pure engineering.
Gujarat served as a laboratory for initiatives between 2001 and 2014 under then Chief Minister Narendra Modi, pioneering national schemes like Swachh Bharat and Jal Jeevan Mission.
The Delhi Declaration of October 2018 established the 4 Ps: Political leadership, Public financing, Partnerships, and People’s participation.
The study recommends linking source and supply, planning before demand arises, promoting water reuse for industries, and strengthening community ownership via Pani Samitis.

Challenges identified include institutional fragmentation between the CWC and CGWB, low wastewater recycling rates of about 30%, and the difficulty weaker administrations face in replicating top-level political priority.
Proposals include merging surface and groundwater bodies into a National Water Commission as recommended by the Mihir Shah Committee in 2016.
sum.text:
New Delhi has hosted the ninth India International Water Week on climate-resilient water management . A new case study says India’s reforms, first tested in Gujarat, offer the Global South (developing countries) four lessons: lead with governance, manage resource and service together, root action in communities, and build for scale.
What water governance is: Water governance is the leaders, budgets, institutions and communities deciding how water is shared and maintained. Like a school, it needs teachers, not just a building.
The study: ‘From Gujarat to India: Water Lessons for the World’ traces water reforms from 2001 to 2026 using official data and practitioner consultations.
Central finding: Water security is as much a challenge of governance and institutions as of engineering.
Gujarat as laboratory: Gujarat’s initiatives from 2001 to 2014 , under then Chief Minister Narendra Modi, piloted later national programmes: Swachh Bharat Mission (sanitation) and Namami Gange (cleaning the Ganga); Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) (household tap water) and Jal Shakti Abhiyan (water conservation); Atal Bhujal Yojana (community groundwater management) and Per Drop More Crop (efficient farm irrigation).
Atal Bhujal Yojana (community groundwater management) and Per Drop More Crop (efficient farm irrigation).
The takeaway: India’s shift from suffering climate shocks to preparing for floods and droughts rests on institutions, not hardware.
Delhi Declaration: The Prime Minister and the United Nations (UN) Secretary-General set out the ‘4 Ps’ in the Delhi Declaration of October 2018 .
Political leadership: Leaders keep water a priority. Eg. Universal tap water and a cleaner Ganga.
Public financing: Public and private money funds both the capital costs of building systems and the recurring costs of running them.
Partnerships: Governments at all levels work with community groups, knowledge bodies and multilateral development banks (lenders owned by many countries) such as the World Bank .
People’s participation: Communities take local water decisions. Eg. Villages resolving to become open-defecation free or preparing village water security plans .
Source and supply linked: Taps and canals fail if water does not flow, so sources and services must be developed together.
Plan before demand: Fast-growing African cities will soon need more water, and planning now costs less than retrofitting.

explain.headline: Resistance to data centres in India requires proactive policy measures
static: Data centres are physical facilities that organizations use to store, process, and distribute large amounts of critical data and applications.
The exponential growth of cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and digital services has driven massive demand for new data centre investments.
Data centres require continuous high-capacity power supply and extensive cooling systems, often relying heavily on local electricity grids and water resources.
India has emerged as a major regional hub for data centres, driven by data localization norms, rapid smartphone penetration, and digital adoption.

Senior advocate Vikas Singh sought the immediate suspension of CEC Gyanesh Kumar, which the Court declined ex parte while issuing notice for a hearing.
The Chief Justice observed that ECI decisions must be unanimous or decided by majority, and the Court can declare contrary actions ultra vires.
Section 18 of the 2023 law specifies that the Commission's substantive business should be unanimous or decided by majority.
Internal records showed Commissioner Joshi objected in May to adding SIR requirements to Form 6 via administrative direction, arguing statutory rules required amendment.

sum.text:
FOR months, the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls has put the voter on trial. On Monday, the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) own decision-making came under scrutiny before the Supreme Court. The Court was hearing petitions arising from reports that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded objections on at least 14 occasions to decisions or actions taken in the name of the Commission.
Senior advocate Vikas Singh sought the immediate suspension of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar. The Court rightly declined such an extraordinary step ex parte and on the basis of newspaper reports. But what the Bench said next was more important.
Chief Justice Surya Kant observed that the Commission’s decisions are expected to be unanimous; where unanimity is not possible, the majority must prevail. Justice Joymalya Bagchi stated that if records show particular decisions were taken contrary to this requirement, the Court could injunct them and declare them ultra vires. A notice has now been issued — for proving the wrongdoing, those concerned must be heard.
But the controversy has changed fundamentally. The question is no longer merely whether SIR was a sound administrative exercise. A prior question has arisen: were some disputed actions legally decisions of the ECI at all?
Section 18 of the 2023 law is clear. The procedure for transacting and allocating the Commission’s business may be regulated by unanimous decisions. Its substantive business should, as far as possible, be unanimous; when Commissioners differ, the majority decides.
The principle is older than the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act. The CEC is the chairman of the Commission, not its commander. The Supreme Court said as much in the TN Seshan case.
In a three-member constitutional body, two constitute the majority. Differences within a collegiate institution are normal, even healthy. What matters is what happens afterwards.
If one Commissioner proposes A and the other two record B, A cannot be labelled as the decision of “Election Commission of India”.Consider Form 6. It is a statutory form under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. Internal records cited by The Indian Express showed that Commissioner Joshi objected in May to adding SIR requirements through an administrative direction, saying that alteration of a statutory form required amendment of…

points: The Election Commission of India (ECI) faces unprecedented public criticism and legal challenges following internal rifts and controversial decisions regarding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
Internal friction became public when 14 letters written by two Election Commissioners revealed cracks in the organisation and pushed the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) into a storm.
The Supreme Court admitted petitions seeking the suspension of the CEC for authoritarian ways, while the Chief Justice of India reportedly noted that no modified Form 6 was approved by the court.
The ECI initially claimed unanimity and later caused confusion by admitting it used two versions of Form 6 for SIR and non-SIR purposes before withdrawing the declaration attached to Form 6.
Supporters cited paragraph 152 of the Supreme Court's May 27 judgement, arguing the court recognized the ECI's residual authority to formulate a documentation framework suited for the SIR.
Critics question why an Election Commissioner termed the Form 6 changes illegal and unauthorised nearly three months after the Supreme Court order if legitimacy was derived from it.
The ECI must make public the minutes of the relevant meeting if it wants people to believe the decision to conduct the SIR was unanimous.

Internal letters indicate the dispute involved alleged illegalities in changing Form 6, denying access to ECINet to registration officers, and excluding commissioners from key decision-making processes.
The author concludes that while the ECI faces a tragic crisis for Indian democracy due to its own actions, institutional redemption depends on accountability and course correction.
sum.text:
The Election Commission of India (ECI) is in a bind like never before . That it worked hard to get here is a pity. An organisation that endeared itself by its friendly approach over the years finds itself friendless. Its only friend, the ruling party, pushes it further into a corner each time it comes to its defence.
The ECI is under attack from almost all quarters — people, civil society organisations, retired civil servants, former judges, practising lawyers, political parties. The print media has written hard-hitting editorials against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), and YouTubers have ready-made content as the ECI rides through this mire of its own making. The “war within” the ECI is in the public square with the Indian Express revealing cracks in an organisation in which confidence is crumbling. The 14 letters by the two Election Commissioners (EC) have pushed the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) in the eye of the storm, even if the storm might rock their boats too. Every attempt of the ECI to explain away the controversy drags it deeper into the morass.
With high courts questioning some of its decisions, serving judges exhorting against mass disenfranchisement, former ECs/CECs questioning its conduct, the clouds over the ECI become thicker. The Shakespearean platitude, “when sorrows come, they come not single spies, but in battalions”, seems to be playing out, with petitions seeking the suspension of the CEC for his authoritarian ways admitted by the Supreme Court (SC).
As if this wasn’t enough, hearing the petitions on October 5, the Chief Justice of India reportedly observed, “No modified Form 6 has been approved by us”. It is these modifications in Form 6 that one of the ECs termed “illegal and unauthorised” in his letter of August 14.
The ECI’s responses to the Indian Express report added to its miseries. The first response on September 23 was “I plead not-guilty”, claiming all decisions were unanimous. In its second response of September 26, the ECI climbed down but created confusion by admitting it used two versions of Form 6 for SIR and non-SIR purposes, asserting the SC “upheld” the changes. Soon, the ECI wilted and withdrew the declaration attached to Form 6 as if it was hiding the weapon used in the crime.

The core issue is the rise of moral policing by radical outfits and self-styled wardens who attack content creators, particularly women and gender minorities, under the guise of preserving culture.
Sandhu, who ran a unisex salon and posted lifestyle reels, had previously faced threats from a Nihang jathedar who claimed his appearance corrupted youth culture.
Prior to his death, Sandhu was the third influencer targeted in Punjab over the last 16 months, following the deaths of Manjeet Kaur and Kanchan Kumari.
Groups like Qaum De Rakhe and Tarna Dal 96 Crori have actively engaged in moral policing, forcing creators to apologize on camera and filing obscenity complaints.
Critics point out that these self-appointed moral arbiters target easy and unarmed victims while ignoring systemic issues like drug addiction and unemployment.
Despite Sandhu's community service during the 2025 floods and his popularity, he became a victim of violent intolerance.
The author argues that such policing contradicts historical Sikh ethos of inclusivity, divinity in all, and the welfare of all.
sum.text:
I n India, the crime of being unapologetically yourself can become your death sentence. It’s a struggle to understand who exactly was offended so grievously by Mad Sandhu, the LGBT make-up artist and influencer who was killed by two motorcycle-riding assailants on 3 October in Amritsar. In the last fortnight of his life, 30-year-old Sandhu’s Instagram feed is like the innocuous diary of any Tier-II-city entrepreneur: lip-sync clips, HydraFacial offers for Manelane, the unisex salon he ran in the city, and “GRWMAD” videos. These offer a little glimpse into the life of the joyful young man. A few days ago, dressed in a flowy salwar-kameez, Mad Sandhu, whose real name was Madhusudan, posted a reel to “ Gutt farhu koi daler gabru ”, an invitation to a brave Punjabi lad to grab hold of his braid. In the video, liked by 23,000 people, he sashays around his Thar, a possession he was undoubtedly very proud of. When Sandhu had bought the car a few months ago, it had — somehow — immediately emasculated Punjab’s strapping young men. One had even called a Mahindra dealership to express his incredulity and said , “How could you sell it to him? I won’t call it a ‘man’ car anymore, it’s a gay car. Phitte moonh .” Show Full Article

points: Architect Swati Janu argues that the physical spaces built for young children significantly shape their early learning and development.
India operates over a million anganwadis under the Integrated Child Development Services programme launched in 1975.
Most government rooms are built for adults, but Janu designs spaces specifically addressing the world below three feet.
Low-cost interventions include outward-facing bookshelves, blackboard paint walls, tactile boards, and beaded grills acting as counting frames.
In Uttar Pradesh, her studio designed a modular octagonal anganwadi that is earthquake-resistant, water-resistant, and easily dismantled.
A district magistrate in Uttar Pradesh leveraged CSR funding from HCL and Rotary Club to replicate the design at 20 locations.
Along the river in Delhi, a flood-resilient anganwadi was constructed using bamboo, river weed insulation, and solar power in weeks.
In rural Bihar, women are trained using fold-out booklets to build home-based creches with mud and bamboo.
Well-designed anganwadis within walking distance can transform early learning while fostering community spaces for parents.
sum.text:
This is the case architect Swati Janu made at a recent Bachpan Manao masterclass: The spaces we build for our youngest children shape how they learn, and even a modest room can be turned into a place that helps a child grow. Anganwadis are the country's front line for early childhood. India runs well over a million of them under the Integrated Child Development Services, the programme launched in 1975 that reaches children in the years before school across cities, villages and everywhere between.
Janu, founder of the Social Design Collaborative, has spent years working out how to make these spaces serve the children inside them, often on budgets that leave no room for waste. Most rooms are built for adults. Janu designs at two levels, one for grown-ups and one below three feet, the world as a young child actually meets it.
At that lower level go bookshelves with picture books facing outward so children choose their own reading, blackboards they can draw on, pin boards where their artwork goes up. A litre of blackboard paint costs a few hundred rupees and turns any wall into a surface for a child's first letters. Beaded grills, known as Bala elements and developed by Kabir Vajpayee's organisation Vinyasa, double as safety doors and counting frames.
Tactile boards made from fur, grass and scrap material can be swapped on embroidery hoops as they wear. None of this needs expensive infrastructure. Janu is firm that children learn best sitting and playing on the ground, that a good mat often beats costly furniture, and that a room should also hold a calmer, less cluttered corner where a neurodivergent child can step back when the space becomes too stimulating.
The harder problem is building at all inside government systems. Janu is candid about the delays, the permissions, the bureaucratic lethargy. Her answer is to find a champion within the system, an officer who shares the vision and carries it forward.
In Uttar Pradesh, her studio designed a modular octagonal Anganwadi with a local NGO and the Women and Child Development Department. Because permanent structures are slow to approve, it was built to be dismantled, made earthquake and water resistant, and given generous windows and storage. The inauguration itself became a tool.
The district magistrate invited CSR companies, and within six months an agreement was signed to replicate the design at 20 locations, 10 funded by HCL and ten by Rotary Club. The constraints can be sharper still. Along the river in…

points: The mining amendment shifts taxing room from mineral-rich States to the Union, creating recurring Centre-State friction.
Parliament is attempting through ordinary law what the Supreme Court's reading of the State List previously ruled out.
Cancelling dues already levied causes retrospective loss and unsettles State budgets planned around those revenues.
No standing body currently reconciles uniform mineral costs with States' room to tax, as the Inter-State Council last met in 2016.
Mineral shares form a substantial part of non-tax revenue for States like Karnataka at 48 percent and Madhya Pradesh at 41 percent.
Proposed solutions include the Union framing conditions with States via the Inter-State Council and offering transitional compensation for cancelled dues.
Another proposal suggests a rate ceiling on State mineral levies instead of Union approval to keep industrial costs predictable.
The future of the amendment depends on whether the Supreme Court permits a regulatory entry to override a taxing entry.
sum.text:
Recurring disputes: The amendment joins earlier Centre-State disputes over Goods and Services Tax compensation , Finance Commission mandates, the National Education Policy , the Citizenship Amendment Act and All-India Services rules.
Ordinary law against a ruling: Parliament is doing by ordinary law what the Court’s reading of the State List ruled out.
Retrospective loss: Cancelling dues already levied unsettles State budgets planned around them.
No bargaining forum: No standing body reconciles uniform mineral costs with States’ room to tax. Eg. The Inter-State Council last met in 2016.
Consult on conditions: The Union should frame the prescribed conditions for State mineral taxes with States through the Inter-State Council.
Transitional compensation: The Centre should compensate States for cancelled dues over a fixed transition period.
Rate ceiling, not a bar: A ceiling on State mineral levies in place of Union approval would keep costs predictable.
The amendment answers industry’s cost complaint by moving taxing room from mineral-rich States to the Union, against the Court’s reading of where that power lies. Whether the Supreme Court lets a regulatory entry override a taxing entry will decide the States’ planned challenges.

India started building its own supercomputers with PARAM 8000 in the early 1990s. Since 2015, the National Supercomputing Mission (NSM) has turned this into a national network. As of September 2026, India has 40 supercomputers with a combined speed of 68 petaflops (PF).
The topic is in the news because the Council of Scientific & Industrial Research (CSIR) is holding the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave (ESTIC-2026) in New Delhi from 27 to 29 October 2026. Supercomputing is one of its themes.
Definition: Supercomputers are high-performance computing (HPC) systems designed to process complex calculations at exceptional speeds.
How they work: Parallel processing: They combine many processors or computing nodes that work on a single problem at the same time, so they are also called parallel computers. High-speed interconnects: Fast connections between nodes let them exchange data during large-scale computations.
Parallel processing: They combine many processors or computing nodes that work on a single problem at the same time, so they are also called parallel computers.
High-speed interconnects: Fast connections between nodes let them exchange data during large-scale computations.
How their power is measured: Performance is measured in FLOPS (Floating Point Operations Per Second), which counts the calculations done in one second. TeraFLOPS (TF): One trillion calculations per second. PetaFLOPS (PF): One quadrillion calculations per second. ExaFLOPS: One quintillion calculations per second.
Global benchmark: The world’s fastest supercomputer reaches about 2.19 exaflops in 2026, or about 2.19 quintillion calculations per second.
Why India needs them: India generates nearly 20% of the world’s data. Artificial Intelligence (AI), weather forecasting and space research all need heavy computing capacity.

Nodal bodies: It is jointly steered by the Department of Science and Technology (DST) and the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY).
Implementing agencies: The Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC), Pune, and the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru, implement it.

Eligible applicants include citizens who attain 18 years of age on qualifying dates like January 1, April 1, July 1, or October 1.
The Election Commission of India functions as a multi-member body where decisions, as far as possible, must be unanimous or by majority.
Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023 governs the business conduct and majority-view rule of the Commission.

points: The Supreme Court stated it never approved any modifications to Form 6, the statutory application for new voter registration.
The controversy focuses on additional ancestry-related declarations introduced on the online ECINET portal during the Special Intensive Revision.
Petitioners and dissenting Election Commissioners argued that altering statutory forms requires amending the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.
The dispute raises legal questions about whether the Chief Election Commissioner acted unilaterally without following collective decision-making.
Chief Justice Surya Kant demanded official records to determine who authorised the disputed changes to the online voter registration process.
The Election Commission defended its actions, stating the online declaration was an auxiliary requirement specifically for the Special Intensive Revision.
The ECI clarified that the additional declaration was already removed from the portal in states where the intensive revision had concluded.
The Supreme Court issued a formal notice on the petitions to examine whether proper statutory and administrative procedures were followed.
sum.text:
The Supreme Court said it had not approved any modification to Form 6 and sought records to establish who authorised the disputed changes. The Election Commission maintains that Form 6 itself was not modified and that the additional declaration was a separate SIR requirement; it removed the declaration from the online form in states where SIR had concluded. The controversy centres on whether the additional requirements could be introduced without amending the Registration of Electors Rules and whether the EC followed its collective decision-making process.

External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has delivered a blunt assessment of the United Nations, saying the world body has become “largely irrelevant” to decision-making on some of the biggest global crises because of a “gridlocked” UN Security Council.
Speaking at the 5th Kautilya Economic Conclave in New Delhi on Monday, Jaishankar said the UN’s inability to respond effectively to major conflicts and global crises had exposed the limitations of its current structure, according to news agency ANI .
“Where the UN is concerned, it's obvious to everybody by now that the UN is gridlocked,” Jaishankar said, pointing to conflicts in the Gulf, Ukraine and Africa, as well as the Covid-19 pandemic.
He said the problem was closely linked to the structure of the Security Council, whose composition, he said, no longer reflects the wider international community.
“And a lot of it is because the Security Council is gridlocked and the Security Council no longer represents the entirety of the global interest,” he said.
The UN Security Council is the United Nations’ principal body for dealing with international peace and security. It has 15 members — five permanent members with veto powers and 10 elected members.
The permanent members — the United States, Russia, China, France and the UK — can block substantive resolutions through their veto.
The structure has increasingly come under scrutiny as major powers have found themselves divided over conflicts, including the war in Ukraine and crises in the Middle East.
Jaishankar argued that the institution has failed to keep pace with the dramatic expansion of the UN’s membership.
“The UN started with 51 members; it's got almost four times that number today. So, if you have grown four times and you want to keep the old board of management, it's not going to work. It's common sense,” he said.
For India, the issue is not simply about securing a permanent seat on the UN Security Council. New Delhi has argued that the Council itself needs to become more representative of the geopolitical realities of the 21st century.
When the UN was founded in 1945, much of Asia and Africa was still under colonial rule. Today, developing countries account for a large share of UN membership, but their representation in the Council’s permanent structure remains limited.
India has therefore pushed for an expansion of both permanent and non-permanent membership, along with greater representation for Africa.

STOCKHOLM, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Belgian-American particle physicist Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for ground-breaking work creating an observatory to detect some of the universe's most elusive particles, high-energy neutrinos, and how they are created.
Halzen realised that ice at the South Pole could be used to track neutrinos, sometimes known as 'ghost particles' for the way they pass through the Earth and our bodies without a trace, and only interact with matter extremely rarely.
"The messengers bring information from the cosmos," Eva Olsson, of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, told a press conference. "They open the door to distant galaxies and tell us about the processes of exploding stars."
HALZEN HAILED FOR DETECTING 'MESSENGERS FROM THE COSMOS'
The neutrino interactions collected by the IceCube observatory in Antarctica provide researchers with knowledge about how high-energy neutrinos are created, potentially even revealing previously unknown cosmic phenomena, the body said.
"Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument," Mark Pearce, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics, said in a statement.
"His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy."
In 2014, the US-based Smithsonian magazine, dubbed Halzen "Neutrino Man" when giving him one of its ingenuity Awards, acclaiming him for an "amazing experiment (that) heralds the beginning of a new era in astronomy".
It even published a comic illustrating his life: "How One Physicist’s Pursuit of the Cosmos Took Off in Antarctica"
The winners of the Nobel physics prize are selected by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences and receive a prize sum totalling 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million), which is shared among the winners if there are several.
The Nobel Prizes were established under the will of Swedish inventor and entrepreneur Alfred Nobel, whose fortune was built in part on the invention of dynamite. First awarded in 1901, the prizes honour achievements in science, literature and peace, with the economics award added later by Sweden's central bank.
WINNERS FROM EINSTEIN TO BOHR AND THE CURIES
Physics occupied a prominent place in Nobel's will and the prize remains one of the discipline's highest distinctions. Over the decades it has recognised discoveries that have fundamentally reshaped humanity's understanding of the universe.

sum.text:
On Monday, the Supreme Court brought fresh clarity to the controversy over Form 6, the application used by new voters to get their names added to the electoral roll. Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said that the court had not approved any modified version of the form.
Kant was hearing petitions seeking that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar be suspeneded for allegedly taking unilateral decisions about procedures related to the special intensive revision of electoral rolls across the country.
The Election Commission had claimed in a statement on September 26 that a declaration attached to Form 6 for the special intensive revision had been upheld by the Supreme Court.
In June 2025, when the SIR began in Bihar , the Election Commission prescribed a separate Annexure D to accompany Form 6. That declaration dealt with the applicant’s age, residence, citizenship and supporting documents.
When the Bihar SIR was challenged before the Supreme Court, this declaration formed was included as documentation in the petitions contending that the Election Commission had exceeded its powers in the manner in which it had conducted the exercise.
In its judgment on May 27, the court upheld the commission’s right to conduct the SIR and recognised its authority to devise a documentation framework suited to such an exercise, subject to limits under the law.
But in July, a modified declaration introduced after that judgment, asked new applicants whether they themselves, a parent or a grandparent appeared on an earlier SIR roll. It sought details of that old electoral entry.
This declaration appeared when new voters filled out Form 6 on ECINet , the Election Commission’s online platform for voter registration and related services. Though this declaration was not part of the prescribed Form 6, applicants could not complete the online form without responding to it.
That is why its legal basis, and the authority under which it was added to the filing process, became important.
Form 6 is prescribed by Rule 13 of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 . It is part of the legal framework governing the enrolment of new voters.
Section 28 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 , gives the Central government, after consulting the Election Commission, the power to make rules on preparing and revising electoral rolls. This includes the forms used for enrolment, which must be notified the official gazette. Those rules are then laid before Parliament.

sum.text: New Delhi: In just two weeks, scientists examining samples from a deep-sea canyon off Argentina identified 57 species previously unknown to science, along with five new genera. Among sea cucumber with horn-like appendages that researchers nicknamed “Loki”.them was a strange The haul came from the Mar del Plata Submarine Canyon, one of the largest deep-sea canyons in Argentina’s waters. The specimens were collected during an expedition in 2025 and examined by 20 taxonomists and early-career researchers at an international species-identification workshop in Buenos Aires this year. The discoveries are remarkable, but perhaps the bigger question is this: how can scientists still find dozens of completely new animals in a part of the planet that covers most of its surface? Show Full Article The answer lies in just how difficult the deep ocean is to reach, observe and study. What was found in the canyon? The 57 new species belong to several very different groups. The scientists identified 20 new copepods, tiny crustaceans that form an important part of marine food webs; 22 echinoderms, including sea cucumbers and crinoids; 14 cnidarians, including corals and sea pens; and one new scaphopod mollusc. Five previously unknown genera were also identified among the specimens. One of the most striking animals was “Loki”, a deep-sea sea cucumber of the genus Peniagone. It gets its nickname from horn-like appendages that reminded researchers of the Norse god. It was found at about 2,577 metres below the surface, in a world where there is no sunlight and pressure is hundreds of times greater than at sea level. And even this collection does not represent everything scientists brought back. According to Argentina’s National Scientific and Technical Research Council, researchers examined only about 10 per cent of the copepod samples collected during the expedition. Some coral specimens could also represent new genera or even a new family, although genetic work is still required to establish that. In other words, 57 is not necessarily the end of the discovery story from this one expedition. Why was this particular canyon so rich in life? The Mar del Plata Canyon sits in an unusually dynamic part of the South Atlantic. Two major ocean currents meet in the region: the warm, salty Brazil Current and the colder, nutrient-rich Malvinas Current. sum.text:
New Delhi, Oct 6 (PTI) The Centre has notified 375 permissible works under the new rural employment framework, with a greater emphasis on livelihood infrastructure, water security and disaster preparedness, expanding the list of works by 41 per cent over the previous scheme.
The Ministry of Rural Development said the new schedule, under the Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (VB-G RAM G) Gramin Act, 2025, divides the works into four categories -- water security, core rural infrastructure, livelihood-related infrastructure, and special works for extreme weather events and disaster preparedness.
Of the 375 works, 128 fall under water security, 111 under core rural infrastructure, 98 under livelihood-related infrastructure and 38 under disaster preparedness, according to the ministry.
The expanded list includes water conservation and irrigation structures, rural health and community facilities, agro-processing units, cold storage infrastructure and flood protection works.
The ministry said livelihood-related works would account for 26 per cent of the total, compared with 1.1 per cent under the previous framework.
These include cleaning, grading and packaging units, mini flour mills, market yards, dairy infrastructure, mushroom cultivation sheds and aquaculture structures.
Infrastructure for self-help groups and their federations, including SHG worksheds and SHE Marts, as well as training and skill development centres, has also been included.
Water security remains the largest category, covering check dams, recharge shafts, rejuvenation of rivers and water channels, reclamation of waterlogged land and rainwater harvesting.
The schedule also provides for drip irrigation, sprinkler systems and interventions such as artificial glaciers for water conservation.
The core infrastructure category includes solar street lighting, waste recycling plants, greywater treatment units, rural libraries, veterinary and rural health centres, Common Service Centres and additional classrooms and laboratories in government schools.
Repair and maintenance of Jal Jeevan Mission water-supply infrastructure is also covered.
For the first time, the framework has a dedicated category for disaster preparedness and extreme weather events. The 38 works include flood relief shelters, embankment strengthening, flood protection, restoration of rural roads and community assets after disasters, and forest-fire management measures, the ministry said.

sum.text:
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has decided to award the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics to Francis Halzen “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.” Halzen realised that ice at the South Pole could be used to track particles known as neutrinos, according to the Nobel Prize website, which added that his vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory – a cubic kilometre of ice that is equipped with light sensors. Using IceCube, researchers can capture neutrinos from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe. “Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument.
His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy,” nobelprize.org quoted as saying Mark Pearce, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics. Neutrinos and Halzen's workNeutrinos are everywhere, yet they rarely reveal their presence, the Nobel Prize website page announcing the Physics award states. Neutrinos pass through the Earth and our bodies without being noticed.
Only on rare occasions does a neutrino interact with an atomic nucleus, creating a detectable signal that scientists with the right equipment can observe. Scientists have long known that the universe contains natural particle accelerators capable of producing particles with energies up to a million times higher than those achievable in laboratories on Earth. However, much remains unknown about these cosmic accelerators: what they are, where they are located and what processes take place inside them.
Extremely high-energy neutrinos are produced in the same environments as other particles. But unlike other particles, neutrinos can travel to Earth without changing direction or losing energy. This makes them a unique source of information about the universe, providing insights that cannot be obtained in any other way.
In 1988, Francis Halzen first proposed his vision of detecting neutrinos at the South Pole. When a neutrino collides with an atomic nucleus, it produces a flash of light that can be detected by sensors embedded in the clear glacial ice. The South Pole offers several advantages for such an experiment: the ice is free from several forms of interference and the region is geologically stable, with no earthquakes.

The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Tuesday approved setting up of a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV), namely, the Integrated Transport & Logistics Authority (ITLA), to strengthen research, planning, appraisal, monitoring and impact assessment within the broad domains of Transportation and Logistics.
According to a release, the approval seeks to address the long-standing challenges arising from fragmented planning and implementation across multiple transport-related Ministries and agencies. By fostering greater coordination and multi-modal integration, ITLA is expected to enhance the efficiency, sustainability and effectiveness of transport infrastructure development in India.
ITLA would have several key roles and responsibilities. It will function as the apex body for integrated transport and logistics planning, research, project appraisal and monitoring, policy support and data analytics.
It will prepare a comprehensive National Transport Master Plan with a planning horizon of ten years or more, covering roads, railways, ports and shipping, civil aviation, inland waterways, coastal shipping, urban mobility and logistics. ITLA will evaluate short-term sectoral plans (5 years or so) and annual plans of transport Ministries to ensure consistency and alignment with the National Transport Master Plan and promote multi-modal infrastructure development.
ITLA will undertake technical appraisal of infrastructure projects of the Government of India, costing Rs.500 crore or more. Financial appraisal will continue to be carried out through the existing financial appraisal mechanisms.
ITLA will monitor implementation of transport & infrastructure projects above Rs.500 crore and provide a coordinated mechanism for issue resolution and will undertake post-implementation impact assessment of these projects.
ITLA will build a unified transport data repository by obtaining relevant transport and logistics datasets from multiple sources, including GSTN e-way bill, FASTag, Vahan, GPS-based systems, urban traffic management systems and other relevant databases and carry out data analytics (e.g. Freight Flow/O-D analytics) for planning, monitoring and impact assessment. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Wednesday announced its latest monetary policy decision, raising the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5% from 5.25%. The central bank also changed its policy stance from ‘neutral’ to ‘calibrated tightening’.The repo rate is one of the RBI’s key monetary policy tools and influences borrowing and liquidity conditions in the financial system. But what exactly is the repo rate, how does it work, and what does an RBI rate hike mean for ordinary borrowers and consumers?
Also read: RBI raises repo rate by 25 points in first hike in four years, loan EMIs may riseWhat is repo rate? Repo is the short form of repurchase agreement. It is a short-term, collateralised borrowing arrangement in which one party sells securities to another and agrees to buy them back at a predetermined date and price.
The repo rate is the annualised interest rate charged on the funds transferred from the lender to the borrower. In simple terms, it is the rate at which the RBI lends money to commercial banks. In return, commercial banks sell government securities to RBI with an agreement of repurchase at a predetermined price and time.
A repo has two parts: the initial sale of securities and their repurchase at a later date. The difference between the two prices reflects the cost of borrowing, or the repo interest. Also read: RBI Repo Rate Hike: What does a 25 basis point increase mean for your home loan EMI?Who fixes the repo rate?
The repo rate cannot be calculated using a simple formula. The rate is determined based on the prevailing economic and money-market conditions. The RBI is responsible for the repo rate.
The Monetary Policy Committee of RBI decides repo rate after carefully examining the market conditions such as, inflation, economic condition and the value of currency. The committee also conducts a meeting in every two months to examine the market conditions. When deciding the repo rate, the RBI looks at factors such as inflation, liquidity in the financial system, borrowing conditions and other money-market rates.
It then decides whether to raise, reduce or keep the rate unchanged. Henceforth, repo rate can be effectively used for controlling, inflation and liquidity of the economy. Also read: Will the RBI repo rate hike push up home loan EMIs, put pressure on housing affordability and festive demand?

sum.text:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday rejected a plea seeking directions to make recitation of the Preamble to the Constitution mandatory during morning assemblies in schools across the country.
A bench comprising Justices Vikram Nath, Sandeep Mehta and AG Masih declined to interfere with the matter and dismissed the petition.
The petition had sought a direction to all schools to mandatorily recite the preamble to the constitution during their morning assemblies.
The petitioner argued that reciting the Preamble in schools could help students understand and imbibe the constitutional values and principles enshrined in it.
However, the Supreme Court refused to issue such a direction and said it would not intervene in the matter.
The preamble declares India to be a 'Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic' and sets out the constitutional objectives of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.
The ruling comes in the context of recurring demands for greater constitutional awareness among schoolchildren, including through educational activities and assemblies.
However, the court's decision means that there is no nationwide judicial mandate requiring schools to include Preamble recitation in their morning assemblies.

The meeting -- to be chaired by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman and comprising representatives from the Centre and states -- is expected to discuss a series of process reforms aimed at making GST compliance easier for businesses and taxpayers. Reports claim that the Council is likely to consider changes to the registration, returns and refunds mechanisms as well as reforms to resolve GST disputes and improve the flow of input tax credit with the aim of reducing the time and cost of compliance. Moreover, the proposals are part of broader recommendations of the GST Council's Law Committee which has examined ways to simplify GST laws and distinguish between deliberate tax evasion and cases where failure to pay tax was not intentional. Under the current GST framework, the Commissioner can authorise an arrest under Section 69 of the Central GST Act where there are reasons to believe that a person has committed specified offences under Section 132, including certain cases involving tax evasion and fraudulent input tax credit. The Council is also expected to discuss measures aimed at making compliance easier for businesses, including e-commerce suppliers. Notably, Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday said the next phase of GST reforms would make compliance easier and improve the refund process, giving businesses greater confidence to invest and expand. Similarly, Finance Minister Sitharaman has said the next phase of GST reforms would focus on simplifying registration, returns, refunds, dispute resolution and input tax credit processes. The GST Council meeting was originally scheduled for September 12 but was postponed to October 7 due to the BRICS summit hosted by India in New Delhi on September 12 and 13. The latest postponement is the second rescheduling of the meeting.

"We will examine all the decisions. If any decision is not in accordance with the law, we will annul it. You know the power of the court," a bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said, as it pointed out that the immunity granted to the CEC is something which even judges don't have.
The bench said that "any modification to Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let's be clear. When records are produced, we would like to see who has modified it".

Mumbai, Oct 6 (PTI) The Reserve Bank of India will announce its bi-monthly monetary policy on Wednesday, with several experts expecting a rate hike after nearly three-and-a half years as inflation pressures rise due to the continuing West Asia conflict.
Reserve Bank Governor Sanjay Malhotra will announce the rate decision at 10 am on Wednesday after the conclusion of the three-day meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee.
A hike in the short-term lending rate (repo) by the RBI in its upcoming monetary policy would mark a stance reversal, following four rate cuts totalling 125 basis points in 2025 and a prolonged pause thereafter.
The last repo rate hike was in February 2023, when the RBI raised the rate by 0.25 per cent to 6.50 per cent. It kept the rate unchanged through 2023-24 before beginning its rate-cut cycle in 2025.
Currently, the RBI's policy repo rate stands at 5.25 per cent.
A majority of participants in a PTI poll expect a 25 bps rate hike with a hawkish tone at the upcoming policy review on Wednesday. The opinion seems divided on whether there will be a shift in stance.
Most experts opined that while a rate increase was imminent, some were of the view that the central bank may not go for a rate hike immediately.
The government has mandated the central bank to ensure that consumer price index (CPI) based retail inflation is at 4 per cent with a margin of 2 per cent on either side.
India's retail inflation accelerated to 4.82 per cent in August from 4.45 per cent in July. PTI NKD DRR

sum.text:
In a significant move to strengthen supply security of critical minerals, the Ministry of Mines has approved 58 companies as eligible participants under its incentive scheme aimed at promoting recycling of key minerals.
The initiative, launched under the National Critical Mineral Mission with a total outlay of ₹1,500 crore, seeks to build domestic recycling capacity for critical minerals extracted from lithium-ion batteries, e-waste, and industrial scrap. The move is expected to reduce India’s reliance on imports while supporting clean energy and advanced manufacturing sectors.
The Ministry said the scheme, notified in October 2025, received strong industry response during its application window, which remained open until April 1, 2026. Proposals were evaluated by the Jawaharlal Nehru Aluminium Research Development and Design Centre, acting as the Project Management Agency.
Following the assessment, the Executive Committee cleared 58 companies in two phases – 20 entities in March and 38 in April. Together, these firms have pledged a combined recycling capacity of around 850 kilo tonnes per annum (KTPA) and an investment of nearly ₹5,000 crore.
The selected companies span key segments such as battery recycling, e-waste processing, and recovery of valuable materials from industrial waste, reflecting growing industry interest in building a robust recycling ecosystem.
The government said the next phase of the scheme will focus on project execution, where eligible entities will receive financial support based on their progress in developing recycling capacity and commencing operations.

explain.headline: Supreme Court 7-Judge Bench May Close Legislative Privilege vs Free Speech Case
static: Legislative privileges are special rights and immunities enjoyed by houses of Parliament and state legislatures, and their members, to enable them to function effectively.
Article 105 of the Constitution deals with the powers and privileges of Parliament, while Article 194 deals with the powers and privileges of state legislatures and their members.
In India, legislative privileges are not explicitly codified into a comprehensive single statute, and largely trace their roots to the practices of the British House of Commons.

When legislative privilege conflicts with fundamental rights like freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a), the judiciary examines the boundaries to ensure fundamental rights are not unduly overridden.

sum.text:
NEW DELHI: Nearly 23 years after it stayed the arrests of some journalists following the Tamil Nadu assembly passing a breach of privilege resolution against them, the hearing scheduled before a seven-judge Supreme Court bench Wednesday, which promised to be a legal duel over the media's right to free speech versus the ambit of legislative privilege, appears to be an exercise for the records. For TN assembly, senior advocate Raju Ramachandran, flanked by attorney general R Venkataramani and solicitor general Tushar Mehta, told a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that the cause of action for the writ petition did not survive and the issue had become academic as the assembly withdrew the resolution imposing 15-day sentence on some journalists in 2004. A bench of CJI Kant and Justices Aravind Kumar, Prashant Kumar Mishra, Joymalya Bagchi, Vipul M Pancholi, Shree Chandrashekhar and V Mohana is scheduled to take up the petitions filed by N Ravi and S Selvam, then editors of 'The Hindu' and 'Murasoli' newspapers, respectively.
Following the Nov 7, 2003, assembly resolution, arrest warrants were issued against the two editors and some journalists. CJI Kant said a seven-judge bench would assemble Tuesday, take the 2004 resolution on record and dispose of the petitions. Pendency in SC has increased to over 90,000 cases.

The approach paper is available on the MoSPI’s website. Comments and suggestions can be submitted by October 16, 2026.
The services sector has firmly established itself as the primary engine of India's economic growth, driving more than half of the national Gross Value Added (GVA).
To monitor this vital performance accurately, MoSPI initiated a monthly compilation of the ISP for the formal sector with 2024-25 as the base year on a trial basis in July 2026.
The initial framework tracks 19 broad service sub-sectors, relying on high-frequency administrative data sources and data on outward supplies from GST, which collectively accounted for approximately 60 per cent of services-sector GVA.
However, core government tasks, non-market activities and GST-exempt services are excluded from the present framework.
To bridge these gaps and build a truly comprehensive Index of Services Sector, the ministry intends to expand the scope of ISP further.
With this aim, MoSPI has published an 'Approach paper on Expanding the scope and coverage for the Index of Services Production'.
The approach paper details methodologies to onboard three major service areas that were previously left out -- Education, Human Health and Residential Care, and Public Administration and Defence.
Together, these three vital sectors represent nearly 21 per cent of services GVA for the 2024–25 period.
By successfully incorporating them, MoSPI will elevate the total coverage of the monthly ISP to approximately 78.4 per cent of the entire services-sector GVA.
This expanded framework will enable aggregation of the sub-sectoral indices into a unified, all-encompassing Index of Services Production that provides a representative reflection of short-term movements of India's services sector. PTI KKS KKS BAL

sum.text:
Madhya Pradesh chief minister Mohan Yadav on Wednesday released two cheetahs, Vyom and Neera, in the Veerangana Durgavati Tiger Reserve (VDTR) in Sagar district, marking the first time cheetahs have been introduced into the reserve. Both cheetahs were brought from Kuno National Park. “Five soft release bomas (built within the release area to allow cheetahs to adjust gradually to their new environment) have been prepared for them in the Muhali range.
Security and monitoring arrangements have been made in an area of about 439 hectares,” field director Rajneesh Singh said. Speaking at the release programme, the chief minister said, “Cheetahs never have any conflict with humans. They live very peacefully.” “If vultures are found anywhere in the largest numbers in the country, it is in Madhya Pradesh.
This is a matter of fortune for us. If tigers are found anywhere in the largest numbers in the country, they too are in our own state. Similarly, there are gharials in Chambal,” the CM said.“I am releasing two cheetahs today, but next month we will bring two more.
These four will expand their family. They will emerge in a new way, in a new era,” the CM added. Spread over 2,300 sq km, VDTR is home to around 30 tigers and 40 leopards.
Experts said it would be a great experience for African cheetahs to co-exist with them. African cheetahs were translocated for the first time in India in September 2022. As many as eight cheetahs from Namibia, 12 from South Africa and nine cheetahs from Botswana were translocated.

Bihar chief minister Samrat Choudhary ordered authorities to provide a thorough report as soon as possible, after reviewing the state's flood situation and the devastation it caused. A news release states that BJP national president and MP Nitin Nabin attended the review meeting, which took place in the "Sankalp" auditorium at Lok Sevak Awas. During the meeting, water resources department secretary Dr Chandrashekhar Singh briefed Choudhary on the causes of the floods and the situation that developed in the state in two phases.
In the first phase, the Ganga, Son, Ghaghra, Kosi and Punpun rivers recorded their highest-ever water levels compared with previous records. During the second phase, excessive rainfall led to the Gandak River reaching record water levels at four locations. Embankment damage was reported at six locations across West Champaran, Gopalganj and Saran districts.
Santosh Kumar Mall, Principal Secretary of the Disaster Management Department, gave a briefing to the group about the relief and rescue efforts conducted during the floods. According to Choudhary, this year's extraordinarily high water levels in the Ganga, Gandak, and Son rivers compared to prior years created a major flood situation. He also identified silt accumulation in riverbeds as one of the major factors contributing to the floods.
The Chief Minister noted that Bihar was the first state in the country to formulate a silt policy. In order to expedite relief, rehabilitation, and necessary development work in affected areas, the chief minister instructed officials to keep a close eye on the current state of rivers and the damage caused by the floods. He also ordered that a preliminary detailed report on the damage caused by the floods be submitted as soon as possible, according to ANI report.
On October 12, 2026, Choudhary announced that households impacted by the second phase of the floods will get ex-gratia assistance. Additionally, he instructed the Disaster Management Department to work with all relevant agencies to evaluate the damage caused by the floods and the estimated cost of repair, and to submit the report as soon as possible. In light of potential issues, officials were also instructed to make the required preparations following the draining of water from flood-affected regions.

sum.text:
Supreme Court Attendance Verdict: A three-member bench headed by Justices Vikram Nath, Augustine George Masih, and Sandeep Mehta had reserved their verdict in a series of petitions questioning the decision of the Delhi High Court which ruled that law students shall not be stopped from taking exams or advancing academically just because of their poor attendance record. The BCI and prominent law schools had raised their concerns in the apex court about how the erosion of compulsory attendance regulations would adversely impact the academic discipline, independence of institutions, and professional conduct in legal education.
This controversy stems from a public interest case filed suo motu by the Delhi High Court based on the 2016 suicide of a student of Amity Law School, Sushant Rohilla, who was suffering immensely due to poor attendance that made him repeat the year. Although the High Court issued wide guidelines to prevent universities from stopping students from proceeding academically on the grounds of poor attendance records, the BCI and law schools found these guidelines to be a judicial interference in statutory educational regimes.
On May 26, the Supreme Court had granted a stay on the operation of paragraph 249 of the judgment of the High Court, whereby students of recognised law institutions should not be restricted from sitting for examinations or carrying out other academic pursuits or their career development due to poor attendance records. It was made clear that the stay would operate prospectively.
The Delhi High Court had also ordered the Bar Council of India (BCI) to review mandatory attendance norms for three-year and five-year LLB courses. High Court had said that norms for mandatory attendance should not be applied so harshly as to cause mental stress to students.
The judgement came out of suo motu case of law student Sushant Rohilla who died in 2016. The matter was first taken up by the Supreme Court and later shifted to Delhi High Court.
High Court had also asked educational institutions and universities to set up Grievance Redressal Committees under UGC regulations. It asked UGC to hold consultations regarding its regulations and amendments in relation to student grievances and mental health issues.

sum.text:
BENGALURU, Oct 6 (Reuters) - India's dominant services industry expanded at its fastest pace in three months in September on stronger demand for financial, consumer and digital services, a survey showed on Tuesday, though quarterly growth was the weakest in more than four years.
• HSBC's India Services Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) rose to 55.2 from August's 54.1, but was below a preliminary estimate of 55.8. A reading above 50.0 shows growth.
• September's improvement failed to prevent the July-September average from falling to its lowest since the quarter ended March 2022, painting a less upbeat picture as hiring softened and export momentum weakened.New business - a key gauge of demand - increased at its quickest pace since June. But international demand was less buoyant with export order growth slowing to its weakest in nearly three years suggesting domestic customers provided a firmer foundation for September's acceleration.
• Input cost inflation was its lowest in 10 months while fees charged to customers rose at their slowest pace since June.
• Business confidence improved to a three-month high but remained subdued historically. Only around 16% of firms expected activity to increase over the next year.
• The services upturn, alongside manufacturing growth accelerating to its fastest since February, lifted the India Composite PMI to a three-month high of 55.9 in September from August's 54.3. Still, its quarterly average was the weakest since January-March 2022, tempering the signs of recovery.
(Reporting by Anant Chandak; Editing by Jacqueline Wong)

sum.text:
Ghana is set to formally apply for membership of BRICS, Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa has announced, marking a significant shift in the country's approach to international partnerships.
Ablakwa disclosed this during the official visit of India's External Affairs Minister, Dr Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, to Ghana.
He described the Cabinet decision under President John Dramani Mahama as a move to diversify Ghana's economic base and expand the country's ties with nations in the Global South.
The minister added that Ghana had already reached out to India for assistance with the application process and was optimistic about receiving its backing.
BRICS currently counts Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, South Africa, and the United Arab Emirates among its core members.
Beyond the BRICS announcement, Ablakwa outlined plans for the two countries to deepen their bilateral relationship across a broad range of sectors, including railways, pharmaceuticals, information and communications technology, defence, and agriculture.
Ghana and India also signed two Memoranda of Understanding during the visit, covering agricultural research and training as well as science and technology.
Dr Jaishankar, for his part, said both nations share comparable development challenges and stand to gain from exchanging expertise and knowledge.
He drew parallels between Ghana's Accra Reset, Feed Ghana, and One Million Coders programmes and similar initiatives under way in India, suggesting the two countries have much common ground to build on.
The Indian minister also praised Ghana's role within the African Union and ECOWAS, and called for closer coordination between the two nations at the United Nations, including on the question of reforming the UN Security Council.
Earlier, YEN.com.gh reported that Ghana won a significant international tax arbitration case against Tullow Ghana Limited, with an International Chamber of Commerce Tribunal dismissing the oil producer's claims in full and upholding a tax assessment worth US$393,091,993.70.
The Tribunal, constituted under the ICC Rules of Arbitration, delivered its ruling on Tuesday, 29 September 2026.
The dispute arose from the Ghana Revenue Authority's assessment of taxes on business interruption insurance proceeds received by Tullow.

explain.headline: Karnataka Wildlife Board to Study Tiger Reserve Buffer Zones and Rejects Quarry Projects
static: Tiger reserves in India are governed under the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972, featuring critical tiger habitats as core areas and surrounding buffer zones to reduce human-wildlife conflict.
State Boards for Wildlife are constituted by state governments under the provisions of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, chaired by the respective Chief Minister.
Eco-sensitive zones and buffer boundaries around protected areas are regulated to balance developmental needs with environmental conservation and wildlife corridors.
The Supreme Court of India frequently issues directives concerning the mandatory creation and enforcement of eco-sensitive zones around national parks and wildlife sanctuaries.
explain.what: The Karnataka State Board of Wildlife decided to form a committee to examine the rationalisation of tiger reserve buffer zones and rejected four stone quarrying proposals near the Kappathagudda sanctuary.
explain.why_in_news: A recent meeting of the standing committee of the State Board of Wildlife led to these decisions regarding buffer zones and quarry rejections.
explain.background: State wildlife boards and forest departments regulate activities around protected areas like tiger reserves and sanctuaries to protect wildlife habitats and local communities.
significance: Highlights the ongoing policy debate over balancing strict conservation regulations with the socioeconomic challenges faced by villagers living in buffer zones.
Demonstrates the strict enforcement of Supreme Court orders and central guidelines prohibiting industrial and mining activities near wildlife sanctuaries.
Important for UPSC exam topics relating to environment, wildlife conservation, protected area networks, and judiciary-executive roles in environmental governance.
prelims: Bhadra tiger reserve has a total area of 492.46 sq km with a buffer zone of 599.79 sq km.
Out of Bhadra's buffer zone, 180.34 sq km is notified forest and 419.45 sq km is non-forest.
The standing committee rejected four quarry proposals within 1 km of the Kappathagudda sanctuary boundary.
The rejected quarry proposals belonged to D Surendra Reddy and S Sudheer Reddy.

stories.ai_why: Tiger reserve buffer zones and wildlife conservation issues.

points: The standing committee of the Karnataka State Board of Wildlife decided to form a technical committee to review the forest department's proposal to rationalise buffer zone boundaries across all tiger reserves.
The proposal notes that villagers residing within these buffer zones face multiple regulations, using examples such as Bhadra and Bandipur tiger reserves.

Bhadra reserve spans 492.46 square kilometres with a buffer zone of 599.79 square kilometres, which includes 180.34 square kilometres of notified forest and 419.45 square kilometres of non-forest area.
In the same meeting, the standing committee rejected four building stone quarrying proposals located within 1 kilometre of the Kappathagudda sanctuary boundary.
The quarry proposals, submitted by D Surendra Reddy and S Sudheer Reddy, were rejected based on a report by the Deputy Conservator of Forests in Gadag.
The rejection followed central government notifications and Supreme Court orders that prohibit new quarries within 1 kilometre of a sanctuary's boundary.
sum.text: <p>Bengaluru: The standing committee of the State Board of <a href="https://www.deccanherald.com/wildlife-environment">Wildlife</a> on Monday decided to set up a technical committee to review forest department’s proposal to rationalise boundaries of buffer zone of all tiger reserves.</p>.<p>The committee was given examples of 2 tiger reserves - Bhadra and Bandipur. Bhadra reserve spread over 492.46 sqkm has buffer zone of 599.79 sqkm, of which 180.34 sqkm is notified forest and 419.45 sq km is non-forest.</p>.Less than half the rain, a changing forest: What a dry year near Bandipur reveals.<p>“People of villages in buffer zones are being subjected to multiple regulations,” the proposal said. The panel agreed to the proposal that a committee should study rationalisation of boundaries.</p><p><strong>Panel rejects 4 quarry proposals</strong></p><p>The standing committee rejected 4 proposals for building stone quarrying within 1 km from the boundary of the Kappathagudda sanctuary.</p><p>The committee reviewed three proposals by D Surendra Reddy and one by S Sudheer Reddy. It took note of the report by the DCF, Gadag that as per the notification by the centre and the Supreme Court orders, new quarries cannot be allowed within 1 km from the sanctuary’s boundary.</p>

points: The Keralam government is formulating a special housing scheme to provide homes to all homeless fisherfolk families in the state.
Chief Minister V D Satheesan announced the initiative while inaugurating the distribution of electric scooters to women fish vendors in Thiruvananthapuram.
The initiative aims to empower women fisherfolk, enhance their financial security, and promote self-reliance through targeted welfare programmes.
Under the 'She Scooter' scheme announced in the state Budget, women fish vendors receive electric scooters with a 75 percent subsidy up to Rs one lakh.
The government plans to increase the number of Society for Assistance to Fisherwomen (SAF) units from 1,800 to 3,000 to promote entrepreneurship.
SAF currently has an annual turnover of Rs 157 crore and provides Rs 41 crore to its members as wages and profit shares.
In the first phase of the 'She Scooter' scheme, 100 sanctioned scooters were distributed to women vendors.
The state also aims to develop its 600-km coastline into a major port city and ensure job reservations for youngsters from local fisher families at ports like Vizhinjam.
sum.text:
Thiruvananthapuram, Oct 6 (PTI) The Keralam government is formulating a special scheme to provide homes to all homeless fisherfolk in the state. Announcing the programme here, Chief Minister V D Satheesan said the government aimed to empower women fisherfolk to earn an independent income and achieve financial security and was implementing various schemes for their self-reliance. “Every homeless fisherfolk family in the state will be provided a house, and a special housing scheme will be formulated for this purpose,” he said after inaugurating the distribution of electric scooters to women fish vendors and a meeting of women fisher entrepreneurs organised by the Society for Assistance to Fisherwomen (SAF) here on Monday.
